query: For a high-entropy alloy initially designed as a single-phase solid solution, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why it loses toughness or undergoes brittle fracture under mechanical loading in demanding engineering service? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, identify the applicable service and loading boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Intermediate-temperature thermal aging in the as‐cast single-phase AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy induces diffusion-driven segregation and subsequent precipitation of secondary phases at grain boundaries, which in turn reduce ductility and toughness, leading to brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase AlCoCrFeNi eutectic high-entropy alloy designed for a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to intermediate-temperature thermal aging (e.g., 500–600 °C for a controlled time period) to simulate service exposure and provoke potential microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: The test samples would be thermally aged under controlled atmospheres and then mechanically loaded using standard fatigue or fracture toughness tests. A parallel set of as-cast control samples maintained without the thermal aging treatment will serve as the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of secondary precipitates (or intergranular phase evolution) resulting from thermal aging that embrittle grain boundaries or interphase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: At intermediate temperatures, enhanced atomic mobility permits segregation of alloying elements and the nucleation of brittle phases at grain boundaries or within the matrix. These precipitates act as stress concentrators under mechanical loads and promote intergranular cracking, thus decreasing the toughness and inducing brittle failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated as-cast baseline that exhibits ductile deformation with high toughness, the thermally aged alloy will show reduced toughness, earlier crack initiation, and a tendency for brittle intergranular fracture when subjected to identical mechanical loading.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy exhibiting uniform microstructure and superior toughness under standard conditions.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to be most significant under conditions simulating long-term service at intermediate operating temperatures and under cyclic or sustained mechanical loading. The hypothesis is applicable in engineering regimes where moderate thermal exposure and high mechanical demands coincide.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature thresholds, aging durations, and the volume fraction or morphology of the precipitates might vary with slight compositional adjustments, and thus the quantitative impact on toughness suffers from some uncertainty. The sensitivity of the mechanical response to the precipitate characteristics requires further detailed investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi samples: one set subjected to intermediate-temperature aging (500–600 °C for a predetermined time) and another kept in the as-cast state. Conduct high-resolution electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) to characterize microstructural changes, focusing on grain boundaries and any precipitation. Perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness testing, fatigue testing) under identical loading conditions for both sets.
measurements: Grain boundary and phase analysis via TEM/SEM to detect precipitate formation
Load-carrying capacity and crack initiation/propagation assessments under cyclic loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not result in detectable secondary phases or microstructural changes at the grain boundaries, and if the aged samples exhibit fracture toughness and ductile deformation characteristics statistically indistinguishable from the as-cast baseline under similar loading conditions, then the hypothesis that intermediate-temperature aging induces embrittlement via precipitation-mediated mechanisms is falsified.
